title: Keriah: The Mourner's Tear
hookLine: mourners tear a garment or a ribbon
carry: mourners tear their clothes, and bless the true judge

cards: His sons bring him a coat, torn and stained with blood, and ask him to identify it. Jacob knows it at once: Joseph's. He believes his favorite son has been killed by a wild animal.
Genesis doesn't give him a speech. It gives him an act. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Jacob rent his garments."
He tore his own clothes. Jewish mourners still do the same in the minutes before a funeral, sometimes with the help of a rabbi holding a small blade.

teach.b: Keriah means tearing, and it's old. Jacob tears his clothes over Joseph. David tears his when news comes that Saul and Jonathan have fallen.
Job, hearing that his children have died, stands up and tears his robe; you met his friends sitting silent beside him in your third year. Grief in the Bible isn't only felt; it's done with the hands.
The mourner stands, the way Job stood up, and the rabbis learned from his verse that the tear is made standing: you meet grief upright. The tear is on the outer garment, a shirt, a jacket, a blouse.
In some communities the tradition is to tear on the left side, over the heart, for a parent, and on the right for other close relatives.
Some mourners instead tear a black ribbon pinned to their clothes, so the garment itself is spared.
As they tear, mourners say an old blessing: blessed is the true Judge. It's hard to say. It doesn't pretend to understand.
In the worst moment, it still names God. Why tear at all? A loss can rip something open inside a person, and polite clothes can hide it.
Keriah lets the outside match the inside.
Through the days of mourning, the torn garment is worn, a visible sign that says: something is missing, don't expect me to be fine. No explanation needed.

how: Before a Jewish funeral, close mourners perform keriah, tearing an outer garment or a black ribbon while standing and saying the blessing 'blessed is the true Judge' (baruch dayan ha-emet); the torn garment or ribbon is worn during the days of mourning.

games.q: you're Jacob. your sons hand you Joseph's coat, torn and bloody. what does Genesis say you do?
o: give a long speech of grief.
send the brothers to search for him.
games.why: Genesis gives Jacob no speech, only an act: he tears his garments, and mourns.

practice: Let one loss come to mind, a death, or a friendship, a place, a life that didn't happen, and name it quietly without explaining it.

Place a hand over the left side of your chest, where the tear would go, and let the loss be real for a few breaths without hurrying to feel better; if you pray, you can say the old words, blessed is the true Judge.
If grief ever feels like too much to carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
